1:
Two witnesses spend their space on whether the letter belongs in the canon at all. Barnes reports that the authenticity of the second and third epistles was doubted by many in the early church and not fully admitted for a considerable time, the first having always been received; he explains the doubt by their brevity and their private address. Clarke argues the other way from internal evidence, that the language and sentiment so accord with the first epistle that whoever wrote one wrote all three; but he grants that as late as the fourth century these were still counted among writings not received by all, and suggests that as private letters they circulated less.

On the self-description the readings converge. Gill offers two reasons: John’s age, being near a hundred and having outlived all the apostles, or his office as overseer of Ephesus and the Asiatic churches, which he says is the same as an elder and not incompatible with the apostolate. Henry takes the first: the saluter is named by a chosen character rather than by name, and is the elder emphatically, possibly the oldest apostle then living — an elder in ancient Israel was to be reverenced, much more one in the gospel Israel of God. Ellicott infers familiarity from the same fact, the writer being so well known that he calls himself only the old man; Wesley calls it suited to a familiar letter upon a weighty subject. Henry adds that ancient letters opened with salutation and good wishes, and religion consecrates such forms so far as it may, turning compliments into real expressions of life and love.

Who is addressed is less settled. Gill argues the elect lady is a person, not a church, since a church is not usually spoken of so and the writer proposes to see her face to face. Wesley treats the word as a proper name, Kyria, since the title of lady was not then applied to any but the Roman empress and would not suit the apostle’s simplicity and dignity. Ellicott allows the name only as a possibility, and fills in the situation: a mother and her children are addressed, her sister’s children are with the writer, and both mothers are called elect. Robertson leaves it open at the next remove, the children being understood literally or spiritually, and notes the relative pronoun is masculine where the noun is neuter, a construction following sense and embracing mother and children of both sexes.

All take the ground of the love to be the truth itself. Gill denies it is her birth, nobility or riches, and offers three senses — Christ, who is the truth and dwells in believers by faith; the Gospel, the same in one as in another, so that unity of judgment produces unity of affection; or the truth of grace as an inward principle. Barnes says they love the family because they love the truth and see it exemplified, truth having taken a permanent abode in every heart that loves religion. Clarke reads the promise as preservation, God keeping not only the Christian religion but its essential doctrines for ever, and records a strange Armenian reading no other version or manuscript supports. Robertson insists the closing clause is a confident assertion, not a wish; that the salutation resembles the Pastoral Epistles — grace the wellspring in the heart of God, mercy its outpourings, peace its blessed effect — and that the repeated preposition before Jesus Christ is unique, bringing out the twofold relation of man to Father and Son. Wesley divides the three the same way — grace takes away guilt, mercy misery, peace implies abiding in both — and treats faith and truth as synonymous. Both Barnes and Clarke stop at “the Son of the Father”: Barnes finds the emphasis characteristic of John, Clarke that it keeps the miraculous conception in view, which the Gnostics denied.
4:
The commentators cannot agree where the children were found, and none pretends the text says. Barnes observes that the apostle does not tell us how he learned it, that the verb suits either acquaintance or report, and records Grotius’s conjecture that some of the sons had come to Ephesus on business and were met there. Wesley supposes their aunt’s house, on the strength of the letter’s last verse; Ellicott thinks probably at home. Robertson keeps the surprise in the verb, notes that the perfect is our own eureka and marks a continued discovery, and quotes the picture of the writer sitting down at once to write to Kyria, glad that her sons, far away in the great city, were true to their early faith. Clarke fills in the household differently, taking the matron for the mother of a family and probably a widow, since no husband is mentioned, and a deaconess in whose house the travelling evangelists were entertained; the children may be her own, or members of the church under her care, or some of both.

What is agreed is that only some are meant, and Gill makes the point sharply: not all, for good parents have not always good children — Adam had a Cain, Abraham an Ishmael, Isaac an Esau — and God shows his discriminating grace in families by taking some and leaving others. Barnes reads the same limitation in the wording, implying he knew of a part only. Henry turns it into encouragement: it is good to be trained to early religion, children may be beloved for their parents’ sake, and it gave great joy to see children treading in their parents’ steps and likely in turn to support the gospel — a pleasing contrast to the many who spread irreligion among their own children.

On the request Henry finds the manner more remarkable than the matter. What is asked is not a bounty to the writer but common duty, so that he might have commanded outright; but harsher measures are worse than needless where milder will prevail, and the apostolical spirit is the most tender and endearing, so that whether from deference to her rank or from meekness he condescends to beseech. Barnes accounts for the familiarity of the address by the disparity of age, John being then very old and the woman much younger; Robertson notes the verb rendered beseech is the ordinary word for praying. Gill records that the Syriac and Arabic keep Kyria as a proper name, and Clarke takes the mode of address as proof that a person and not a church is written to.

The commandment is old and new at once, and each fixes the beginning differently. Barnes says John presumed it understood as far as the gospel was known, since Christianity never prevails without prompting obedience to this law. Clarke dates it from the first publication of Christianity; Wesley from our Lord’s ministry, adding that in some sense it was from the beginning of the world; Henry allows it may be called new as declared by Christ, while as to the matter it is old. On the definition that follows, Gill takes walking after the commandments as the way love is shown to God, expecting fresh discoveries of God’s love in return; Barnes calls it the evidence of love and the peculiar commandment by which the disciples are distinguished; Clarke states that love is the principle of obedience; Wesley calls universal obedience built on the love of God the proof of true love. Ellicott gives the fullest account, making love the moral disposition that embraces all other virtues — implying faith, since founded on Christian principle and testable only by right belief; purity, since modelled on the love of God; and unselfishness, since it desires another’s good. Robertson leaves undecided whether the closing “in it” refers to the truth, the love or the commandment, thinking love likeliest.
7:
Barnes detaches the opening word from what precedes: the conjunction introduces the warning that follows rather than a reason for mutual love — since many such are abroad, look to yourselves. Henry keeps the connection, hearing a reason for the previous request — you have need to maintain your love, because there are destroyers of it in the world, and those who subvert the faith destroy the love. He adds that sad news may properly be told to Christian friends, not because we love to make them sorry but to forewarn them. Gill describes them by quality and number: deceitful workers pretending to be ministers of Christ while lying in wait to deceive and handling the word of God deceitfully; and many, so likely to do much mischief. Clarke identifies them as Gnostics, since they denied that Jesus was come in the flesh, and observes that none could deny so essential a doctrine but a deceiver and an antichrist. Wesley reads the denial more broadly, of any who disbelieve his prophetic, priestly or kingly office. Robertson notes the word for deceiver means wandering or roving, and is applied in the New Testament to Jesus by his enemies and to Paul.

A textual question runs through the passage. Gill records that the Alexandrian copy, with the Vulgate and Syriac, reads that the deceivers have gone out into the world rather than entered it; Clarke says the same of many manuscripts and judges the sense nearly the same; Robertson takes the going out as the true reading and hears an allusion to the crisis when they left the churches. On the next verse Clarke reports that many manuscripts, versions and fathers put the clause in the second person — that ye lose not what ye have wrought — and calls that more consistent and likely, though he also explains the received text by the apostles fearing to lose their converts as their crown of rejoicing. Robertson settles it the same way, the two verbs being second person while the clause about what was wrought is genuinely first, since John does not wish his own labour lost. Wesley keeps the first person throughout and reads it as modesty, adding that losing what has been wrought is what every apostate does.

On the exhortation Barnes makes a rule of priority: the first care must be to secure one’s own heart, since when error abounds our first duty is not to make war on it but to look to the citadel of our own souls, as an invaded country does not march out regardless of its own fortresses. Gill puts it as bewaring of the deceivers; Robertson compares our phrase, look out; Clarke expands it into watching, praying, loving God and each other, and walking in newness of life.

The last verse turns on two questions of sense. Gill insists the transgression is not of the law of God, of which everyone is a daily transgressor, but of the rule of doctrine; Clarke takes the verb as passing over a sacred enclosure, promising the one who abides within communion with the Father and the Son; Wesley alone keeps the wider sense and refers it to any law of God. On the doctrine of Christ, Barnes finds the phrase as ambiguous as the love of Christ, and cannot decide between the doctrine Christ taught and the true doctrine concerning him, reporting Macknight’s view that it is what Christ and his apostles taught and inclining to it. Robertson decides flatly that it is the teaching of Christ and not teaching about him; and he sets the verse against its first opponents, these Gnostics being the self-styled progressives, anxious to relegate Christ to the past in their onward march, so that the word rendered transgresseth is really going on ahead — often the right thing to do, but shown bad here by the clause beside it.
10:
All the witnesses take the prohibition to concern teachers rather than travellers, and most of them are at pains to say how far it does not reach. Gill reads the comer as arriving under the character of a preacher; Clarke as coming under the character of an apostle or evangelist, to preach in the house, so that the refusal means giving him no entertainment as an evangelical teacher and not letting him preach under that roof; Barnes as any professed teacher of religion, and thinks there can be no doubt this household was accustomed to entertain such men. Henry supplies the likely reason: this lady was possibly like Gaius in the next epistle, a generous housekeeper and hospitable entertainer of travelling ministers, so that these deceivers might expect the same reception as anyone else; the direction is therefore negative, that she is not to support them, since the Lord Christ will distinguish them from his own ministers and would have his disciples do the same. Robertson makes the same distinction from the other side, that John is not speaking of entertaining strangers at all but of deceiving propagandists who carried dissension and danger with them, and notes that the house is definite without the article, like our own at home.

Barnes states the limit plainly: the words cannot mean that no acts of kindness were to be shown in any circumstances, only that nothing was to be done which could fairly be construed as encouraging or countenancing them as religious teachers, and that so far as we meet such men as neighbours or strangers we are to be honest, true and kind. Clarke ends at the same place after a much harder passage: no sound Christian should countenance any man as a gospel minister who preaches erroneous doctrine, and no Christian can attend such a ministry without being criminal in the sight of God — whether the teacher belongs to an established Church or to any congregation of dissenters — but what the apostle says here does not mean that we should deny such men the common offices of humanity, charity and mercy. Wesley draws the line differently, extending the refusal to receiving the man either as a teacher or as a brother.

On why the greeting itself matters the accounts converge on complicity. Clarke explains the idiom, that the words mean do not say Health to him, do not salute him with Peace be to thee, the usual eastern salutation among those of the same religion being one they do not use to strangers; and he gives the reason for withholding it, that treating such a man as a sound Christian brother puts it in his power to deceive others by apparently accrediting his ministry. Gill defines the phrase as wishing him well and success in his ministry, or conversing with him in a friendly and familiar way; Barnes says it shows that one countenances and approves the doctrine taught; Wesley, that whoever gives him any encouragement is accessory to his evil deeds. Robertson supplies the institutional fact that makes the rule intelligible: the churches often met in private homes, so that if these travelling deceivers were allowed to spread their doctrines there and then sent on with an endorsement, as Apollos was sent from Ephesus to Corinth, there was no way of escaping responsibility for the harm they did. It is not, he repeats, a case of mere hospitality to strangers.
12:
The reason for breaking off is read the same way by all, and several draw a lesson from it. Henry calls it an adjournment of many things to personal conference, since some things are better spoken than written: the use of pen and ink may be a mercy and a pleasure, but a personal interview may be more so. He infers from the promise of a visit that the apostle was not yet too old for travel, nor therefore for travelling service, and adds that the communion of saints should be maintained by all methods and should tend to mutual joy — excellent ministers having their own joy advanced by their Christian friends. Clarke reaches the same conclusion more briefly, that there is more comfort in mutual interviews among friends than in epistolary correspondence. Barnes reads the sentence as the language of one who is hurried, or in feeble health, or hoping soon to meet the person written to, so that only the points of most immediate importance are selected and the rest reserved. Wesley says simply that the apostle wrote only what was then peculiarly needful. Ellicott takes a different point from the same words, that this verse shows the letter was not a mere accompaniment to a copy of the First Epistle.

Gill puts the contents of the unwritten remainder to a use of his own. What was left unsaid might concern the state of the churches of Asia and particularly Ephesus, or private families and persons, or the doctrines of the gospel — but not any new doctrine, since the apostle has already denied having any beyond what they heard from the beginning; and Gill concludes that the verse therefore makes nothing for the unwritten traditions of the Papists, as though the Scriptures did not contain the whole of doctrine and of the will of God.

The writing materials draw more comment than one might expect. Barnes warns that the English word paper conveys an idea which is not strictly correct, since paper as now understood was not invented until long after, the material being the Egyptian papyrus. Robertson describes its preparation, the pith cut into strips and pasted together, notes that the word for ink is simply the old adjective for black, and remarks that John apparently wrote this little letter with his own hand; he also gives the closing phrase its literal force, mouth to mouth. Ellicott goes furthest into the manufacture: the ink was a mixture of soot, water and gum, the papyrus grows in the swamps of the Nile to ten feet and more, the paper was made from the thin coats surrounding the plant, and the separate pieces were joined by the turbid Nile water, which has a kind of glutinous property, one layer being laid flat on a board and a cross layer set over it.

The closing greeting leaves one person unaccounted for, and two witnesses notice it. Gill denies that the elect sister means a sister church, as some think, and takes her for a sister according to the flesh, herself chosen of God, whose children were also walking in the truth and now send their salutation to their aunt; he thinks it very likely they lived at Ephesus, where John resided. Barnes observes that nothing more is known of her, and infers from her not being mentioned as sending a greeting of her own that she was probably either dead or absent, while noting that John still names her as one of the chosen of God.
